newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African 1996 gold output lowest in 40 years.
newsitem.headline: S.African 1996 gold output lowest in 40 years.

text.p: South Africa's gold output plunged to a 40-year low of 495 tonnes in 1996 but production should stabilise at around 500 tonnes a year in future, the Chamber of Mines said on Monday.
It said output in the world's largest gold producing country was 494.62 tonnes last year, down 27.8 tonnes from 1995 and only marginally higher than the 494.44 tonnes produced in 1956.
The fall cost South Africa around 1.5 billion rand ($340 million) in lost revenue and foreign exchange earnings, the chamber said.
But Chamber of Mines senior economist Roger Baxter said he did not expect the situation to get any worse.
"We can see that the rate of decline in the industry, the rate of fall in production, is stabilising," he told Reuters.
South African gold output has been declining steadily with rising working costs and dwindling grades chipping away at production in the country.
Baxter said output had dropped from 619 tonnes in 1993 to 584 tonnes in 1994 and 522 tonnes in 1995.
"The rate of fall-off in production has definitely turned and production levels are expected to stabilise at roughly the 500 tonnes level for the foreseeable future," Baxter said.
He said reasons for the drop in production included workplace disruptions, consolidation in the industry, escalating costs and a focus on quality mining at the expense of tonnage.
"Increasing cost pressures with the falling gold price does increase the number of marginal mines and places pressure on profitibality," Baxter said.
Bullion was last trading at around $340.70 an ounce.
Gold analyst Trevor Pearton of stockbrokers Societe Generale Frankel Pollack predicted that production would begin to recover and could lift to around 550 tonnes a few years down the road.
He said South African mining houses increased production in the three months to end-December on average by 4.4 percent.
"That is a reasonable turnaround...I would see our production rising again, probably (on average) at about five or six percent per annum," Pearton said.

Both Baxter and Pearton said South Africa's 120-year-old gold mining industry still had life in it and this showed in a host of new mining projects aimed at gaining access to previously unreachable ore.
Mining giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd is studying establishing two ultra-deep gold mines reaching up to five km (three miles) below the earth's crust.
And other South African mining houses also have projects due to come onstream in future which would lift the country's gold production.
"We certainly have a first-class industry which has been remarkably resilient for the 120-year history that it has.
"It has produced over 47,000 tonnes of gold during its history and there still is a substantial portion of gold that can be recovered," Baxter said.
